summary: Fiji is an island nation in the South Pacific made up of more than 300 islands, whose population is mainly indigenous Fijians and Indo-Fijians; it is known for tropical resorts and rugby.

ranking.name: Methodism
ranking.description: In 1835 the British Methodist missionaries William Cross and David Cargill landed on Lakeba Island in the east and began missionary work in Fiji. In 1854 Cakobau, the most powerful paramount chief of Bau, converted to Methodism, and chiefs and their people in various places then converted en masse, so the church became closely tied to the traditional chiefly system. After Fiji was ceded to Britain in 1874, Methodism became the main faith of indigenous Fijians, and the church still has considerable political influence today.

ranking.name: Hinduism
ranking.description: From 1879 to 1916 the British colonial government used the indentured labor system to bring about sixty thousand workers from India to work on the sugar plantations, and their descendants are the Indo-Fijians, most of whom follow Hinduism. Because of the repeated coups and political turmoil since 1987, large numbers of Indo-Fijians emigrated to Australia, New Zealand and elsewhere, so the share of Hinduism has fallen from more than three-tenths in the past.

ranking.name: Other Christian denominations
ranking.description: These include the Anglican Church, the Seventh-day Adventist Church, and Pentecostal churches such as the Assemblies of God that grew rapidly in the late 20th century. These churches have attracted many young people and city residents, and some believers have moved over from Methodism, making Fijian Christianity more diverse internally.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: In 1844 missionaries of the French Society of Mary (Marists) arrived in Fiji and began a missionary rivalry with the Methodists. The Catholic Church is known for its schools and medical services, and its believers include indigenous Fijians, Indo-Fijians and other Pacific Islanders.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: About one-seventh of the Indian indentured laborers were Muslims, who built mosques and religious schools in the sugar districts, and the Fiji Muslim League was founded in 1926. Muslims are concentrated mainly in the sugar-producing areas of western Viti Levu and Vanua Levu.

religion.background: Indigenous Fijians originally followed ancestral spirits and gods; after Methodist and Catholic missionaries arrived in the 19th century, the conversion of chiefs led to the Christianization of the whole population, and British colonial rule in 1874 further consolidated the position of the church. To develop the sugar industry the colonial government brought in Indian indentured laborers, who introduced Hinduism and Islam, giving Fiji a society in which religion and ethnicity overlap to a high degree: indigenous people are mostly Christians, and Indo-Fijians are mostly Hindus or Muslims. This dividing line is also reflected in the ethnic politics of the several coups since 1987.

language.official: English, Fijian and Fiji Hindi are the official languages.

ranking.name: Fijian
ranking.description: Fijian belongs to the Austronesian family, with many dialects on the various islands. In the 19th century missionaries translated the Bible using the dialect of Bau Island in the east, and together with the political advantage of the chiefs of Bau, the Bauan dialect became standard Fijian. The orthography devised by the missionaries is distinctive; for example, “c” represents the th sound and “b” represents the mb sound. It is the mother tongue of indigenous Fijians, and the 2013 constitution made Fijian, English and Fiji Hindi official languages together.

ranking.name: Fiji Hindi
ranking.description: The indentured laborers brought from northern India between 1879 and 1916 mostly spoke Awadhi and Bhojpuri, which blended on the plantations into a new common language, “Fiji Hindi,” absorbing English and Fijian vocabulary. It is the mother tongue of Indo-Fijians, and because of the large emigration of Indo-Fijians after 1987, the proportion of speakers has declined.

language.history: Fiji was settled more than three thousand years ago by Austronesian-speaking navigators, and hundreds of dialects developed on the various islands. In the 19th century missionaries used the Bauan dialect as the basis for a written Fijian and opened schools. After Fiji became a British colony in 1874, English became the language of administration and education and is still the common language among the different ethnic groups today. The Indian laborers brought in during the colonial period formed Fiji Hindi. After independence in 1970, English, Fijian and Fiji Hindi have coexisted, reflecting the history of Fiji’s diverse ethnic groups.

ranking.name: Kokoda
ranking.description: Fresh white-fleshed fish is diced and marinated in lemon or lime juice until it turns white, then mixed with coconut milk, chili, onion and tomato, and often served in a coconut shell.
ranking.history: Marinating raw fish in acidic fruit juice is an ancient practice of Pacific Islanders; Fiji is surrounded by sea and has abundant catches, and with coconuts everywhere, this refreshing dish arose. The addition of coconut milk is a feature of the Fijian version, similar to comparable dishes in Tonga, Samoa and elsewhere. It is a representative dish of Fijian entertaining and of tourist restaurants and is regarded by many as Fiji’s national dish.

ranking.name: Lovo (earth-oven cooking)
ranking.description: Stones are heated in a pit in the ground, and meat, fish, taro and cassava wrapped in banana leaves are placed in, covered with leaves and earth and cooked for several hours.
ranking.history: Earth-oven cooking is an ancient cooking method shared across the Pacific islands, existing long before Europeans arrived and using the heat retained by the stones to cook a large amount of food at once. In Fiji the lovo is usually the responsibility of men and is used for large gatherings such as weddings, funerals, church events and Christmas, requiring the cooperation of the whole village to prepare. It symbolizes communal sharing and traditional ritual and remains at the heart of important Fijian festivities today.

ranking.name: Palusami
ranking.description: Young taro leaves are wrapped around thick coconut milk and onion, sometimes with corned beef or fish added, and baked in an earth oven or an oven, rich and smooth in texture.
ranking.history: Taro is a traditional staple of Pacific Islanders, and the combination of taro leaves and coconut milk is found in Fiji, Samoa and Tonga as an ancient island dish. Canned corned beef imported in the colonial period was later added as well, becoming the common modern version, reflecting the influence of colonial trade on island food. It often appears together with lovo at Sunday family meals and festive banquets.

ranking.name: Kava (yaqona)
ranking.description: The dried root of the pepper-family plant kava is ground into powder and kneaded in water in a large wooden bowl and strained into a drink that has an earthy taste and leaves the mouth and tongue slightly numb and the drinker relaxed.
ranking.history: Kava is called yaqona in Fiji and is at the core of traditional ceremony: a visitor entering a village must present a kava root to the chief, called “sevusevu,” and may stay only after being accepted. In the 19th century missionaries tried to restrict drinking, but it continued as a social drink and is used in state ceremonies such as visits by members of the British royal family. Today Fijians often sit together to drink it in villages, offices and family gatherings, popularly called “grog,” an important social culture.

ranking.name: Roti
ranking.description: Flour, water and a little oil are kneaded into a dough, rolled into thin round flatbreads and cooked on a flat griddle, soft in texture and often eaten wrapped around curry.
ranking.history: Roti was brought by the indentured laborers who came to Fiji from India between 1879 and 1916 and was originally the daily staple of Indo-Fijian households. Over more than a hundred years, it and curry have become an everyday food of all Fijians, loved by every ethnic group, and “roti parcels,” with curry wrapped in roti, are common at schools and work sites. It embodies the profound influence of Indian immigrants on Fijian food culture.
